units: the object described is a listening accessory set down on a piece of furniture
a colored signal crosses the surface before the charge ends
a short sound announces that the cell is full
the shell shows marks of use along its edges
the hinged joint bends without breaking
the cord stows away in a side compartment
an opening pushes the heat produced toward the rear
the stand can be tilted in successive steps
the whole thing folds small enough to fit at the bottom of a bag
text: Set the earpiece down on the table and watch what comes next. The shell warms up under your fingers first. Then a pale blue band slides across the top, and a soft click says the rechargeable cell has filled. The case is small enough to disappear inside one palm. Its edges have gone dull from handling, and the supple hinge bends over and over without cracking. The wired cord coils beside it and tucks into a pocket along one side. Later, once the shell runs hot, a thin grille pushes the warm air out the back. The adjustable stand lifts one notch, then another, until the angle finally sits right. When the session is over, everything folds away. The base drops into its sleeve, the cord follows, and the whole thing goes flat enough to vanish at the bottom of a bag. Nothing bulky, nothing brittle, nothing to take apart.

units: the text questions the early wearing out of electronic equipment
glued assembly prevents the replacement of a single component
repair shops observe this pattern
whole objects are thrown away although only one joint has failed
manufacturers shorten the period of software support
hardware in good condition becomes unusable without a patch
the buyer bears a double cost
local repairers lose their trade
the author calls for a demountable assembly and available diagrams
the author asks that the cell be replaceable on its own
text: Should we worry that our machines wear out before their time? Repair shops have known the first cause for a long time. Once a case is glued shut instead of screwed, one failed part kills the whole device. You can read the effect in the sorting bins, piled with hulls that lost nothing but a single joint. A second cause piles onto the first one and deepens it. Makers cut short the years of software support, so a perfectly healthy unit turns useless for want of a patch. The buyer pays twice, once for a machine and once for the machine that follows it, and the shop down the street loses the trade that fed it. None of this has to hold, and the whole thing can be turned around. Screws instead of glue, open diagrams, and a rechargeable cell you can swap on its own would hand the repairer back everything the adhesive took.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the main figure is designated by her trade as a repairer
the smell of melted metal stays on her hands after closing time
she began with old dusty sound receivers
those devices came from a woman living nearby
at first she could not identify the failed part
she replaced parts at random and spent her money on it
she took up the habit of writing down every fault
her notebook records the symptom and the part at fault
she now recognizes recurring families of faults
she repairs almost without ever accepting money
text: Her hands hold the smell of melted solder long after the shop closes. The repairwoman started out on dusty radio sets handed down by a woman next door, opening them with no diagram and closing them with no certainty. Her trouble came down to one thing. She could not tell which part had failed, so she swapped components at random and burned through her savings doing it. What rescued her, in the end, was a notebook. In it she sets down every fault, the symptom, the guilty part, the reading she took. The notebook has grown thick and stained, limp from years of thumbing. Now she reads whole families of faults in it, and she guesses before the case is even open. Neighbors from the surrounding streets bring her dead lamps and wired keyboards. She brings them back one at a time, and mostly she turns down the money.

units: two soldering devices are compared
one reaches the wanted heat far faster than the other
this gap weighs on the pace of the workshop
the slower device offers fine adjustment of the heat
the fast device gives only a small number of settings
the massive base of one gives better stability
the other moves as soon as its cord is pulled
the softened lead of one of them absorbs jolts
the other lead stiffens when the weather is cold
one of the two requires costly branded tips
text: Two soldering stations fight over one bench, and the ruling between them comes down to differences you can measure. The first one brings its tip up to the set temperature almost the instant you switch it on. The second dawdles, and that gap drags on the pace of the shop. The slow one, though, dials the heat in by the degree, while the quick one gives you three fixed settings and nothing between them. One base is heavy and eats up a good deal of bench room, yet it never shifts. The other skates the moment you tug on its cord. The lead on the first wears a supple silicone jacket. The second stiffens in the cold and sends every jolt straight to the point. Last of all, one takes ordinary spare tips, and the other demands a costly house brand. For a repair shop, the slow heavy machine wins, waiting and all.

units: the writer addresses the woman in charge of a workshop
the message concerns equipment lent to a group
the embroidery machine now takes the designs sent by the club
its arm sags when facing thick fabric
the jointed support of the lamp no longer holds a high position
the tablet works only once plugged into the mains
its cell no longer lasts a whole session
the rolling cabinet blocks movement in the room
two input devices are missing from the storage cupboard
the writer asks that these remarks be passed to the technical staff
text: To the workshop director, I am writing about the equipment on loan to the assisted sewing group. First, the embroidery machine now takes the patterns the club sends over, but its arm begins to sag as soon as the cloth gets thick. Second, the jointed lamp still gives good light, though its adjustable neck will no longer hold a high position. Third, the tablet lent to the students still works, provided it stays plugged in. Its rechargeable cell no longer covers half a session. Fourth, the rolling cabinet takes up far too much room for this space and blocks the way through it. Last of all, two wired keyboards have gone missing from the dusty cupboard at the back of the room. I would be grateful if you passed these notes along to the technical staff, and I am glad to walk anyone through them.

units: a visitor asks a workshop how an electronic board is made
the layout is first designed on a screen
the pattern is carried onto a metal coated sheet by exposure
the surplus metal is removed in a chemical bath
a guided rotating tool drills the passages meant for the connections
solder paste is laid down before the parts are set in place
the whole is brought to high heat to fix the joints
a camera inspects each board looking for a flaw
this check comes before final assembly
text: A visitor to the workshop starts by asking how a printed board comes into being. The answer runs through the work in the order it is done. It begins as a drawing on a screen, then moves onto a copper clad sheet by exposure to light. What becomes of the copper nobody wants, the visitor asks next. A bath of acid eats it away, and the sheet comes out of it with clean, fine tracks running across it. Then comes the drilling, where a guided cutter opens the holes the pins will sit in. Is the sheet ready to use now? Not yet, because solder paste still has to go down, the parts have to be set in place, and the whole thing has to ride through an oven whose hot air locks every joint. One last question covers the checking. A camera looks over each board and catches the bad track before final assembly.

units: a man from the floor above complains about the running time of his drilling tool
his neighbor blames the fault on the way the device is recharged
the power pack stayed permanently on its charger
the casing of the pack had swollen
a measuring device was used to test the cells one by one
two cells no longer delivered any current
this explains the loss of force while drilling
he is advised to store the pack half charged in a cool place
he must take it off the charger as soon as the green light shows
text: The neighbor from upstairs came down with his drill tucked under one arm, saying over and over that the battery held nothing anymore. My sister told him that the tool itself was innocent, and that the fault lay in his habit of leaving the pack sitting on its hot cradle around the clock. He argued for a while, and then he admitted that the casing had swollen out of shape. So she pulled a wired meter out of the dusty drawer and took a reading on each cell on its own. Two of them were dead, which explained why the power fell away the moment the bit bit into the wood. She told him to store the pack half charged somewhere cool, and to lift it off the charger as soon as the green light comes on. He went back upstairs pleased with himself, with a drill that ran again and a fresh bit thrown in.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the first mechanical looms raised a repeated blockage
changing the pattern required taking the mechanism apart
the threads had to be set again one by one
production stopped for several weeks
customers turned to weavers working by hand
the solution was to put the pattern information outside the machine
a craftsman devised a series of pierced boards linked together
the presence or absence of a hole decided whether the thread rose
changing the design came down to replacing the band
this principle was later taken up by calculating machines
text: In the earliest mechanized weaving shops, one obstacle kept coming back. Every change of pattern meant taking the mechanism apart and threading the yarns again one by one, and output stopped for weeks at a stretch. Orders drifted off to weavers working by hand, slower but far more willing. The way out came from outside the cloth trade, and it was to put the pattern into something that lives apart from the machine. A craftsman thought up small pierced boards, chained into a supple band that the loom read as it went by. Where a needle met a hole, the thread rose. Everywhere else it stayed down. Changing the design now meant changing the band, nothing more. The idea outgrew weaving fast, and that split between the order and the part that carries it out still runs through calculating machines.

units: the antenna is compared to a string that vibrates when a wave passes
the antenna produces no energy by itself
the loudspeaker follows the opposite path
a current sets the cone of the loudspeaker in motion
this motion makes the nearby air vibrate
in one case the energy arrives from outside and becomes electrical
in the other the energy leaves the conductor and becomes sound
both devices cope badly with too harsh a setting
an attracting metal mass bends the signal
text: An antenna is less like an ear than like a taut string stretched at the edge of a river you cannot see. The string makes nothing of its own. It shivers when a wave goes by, and it falls quiet when the wave moves off. A loudspeaker runs that path backwards. Send it a current, its supple cone stirs, and the air around it starts to shake. One listens, one speaks, and both live off the same family of motion. What separates them is the direction of the trade. In the antenna, energy arrives from outside and turns into a faint current. In the speaker, energy leaves the wire and turns into audible breath. One more thing ties them together, and it is that both hate hard matter around them. A stiff mount kills the motion, a magnetized mass bends the signal, and ear and mouth alike go deaf.

units: a failure occurs at night on a backup server
the team examines three subsystems in turn
the power supply shows an abnormal variation of voltage
a damaged capacitor is the origin of this fault
a fan no longer turns steadily
its clogged bearing lets the temperature pass the allowed limit
two storage units contain unreadable areas
no notification had reported these areas
the faulty parts are replaced and the data rebuilt
the lesson drawn is that a silent fault costs more
text: The failure hit in the middle of a maintenance night, on a backup server that the team had always taken for indestructible. They worked their way through three areas, one after another. On the power side, the readings showed odd ripple on the main rail, the mark of a worn, bulging capacitor. On the cooling side, a failing fan turned in fits and starts, and its dusty bearing let the board run well past the allowed limit. On the storage side, two drives reported sectors they could not read, and no warning had ever gone out about them. The repair went down that same list in order. Capacitor replaced, fan swapped for a fluid bearing model, drives rebuilt across the array. The team came away from that night with a lesson that stuck. A silent warning costs far more than a breakdown that makes noise.
